messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 76-year-old European-American man, is a retired hotel manager who has been struggling with the aftermath of toxic chemical exposure he experienced at his workplace. The event occurred several years ago when a cleaning supply spill in the basement released harmful fumes that permeated through the entire hotel. John's experience of the traumatic event was vivid and terrifying; the smell of the chemicals is still etched deeply into his memory, even now. Since then, John has found himself on edge, especially within the confines of his home where he once felt secure. He often feels as if he must be constantly vigilant, a sense that has only intensified over time. The alertness he experiences at home is rooted in a deep-seated belief that his body can no longer be trusted to protect him from danger. This feeling has left John with a profound sense of helplessness, reinforcing the notion that bad things will continue to happen despite his best efforts to prevent them. John's memories of the event are fragmented and disconnected, often surfacing without clear visual imagery but instead as overwhelming emotional sensations. When he thinks about the frightening episode, the smell of the chemicals is acutely present in his mind, causing intense distress. These disjointed recollections have become a trigger for his heightened alertness. He finds himself constantly on guard, particularly when unexpected or loud sounds occur, which only serves to reinforce his belief that his body continues to react as if he is still in immediate danger. To cope with these overwhelming feelings and memories, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. One such strategy involves putting on loud music or TV, hoping the noise will drown out the intrusive thoughts and sensations. He also monitors his own thoughts obsessively for signs of going crazy, a behavior that stems from his belief that his body is unreliable and no longer a safe haven. John's constant vigilance has extended to his daily life as well. He avoids areas where he might encounter similar smells or settings reminiscent of the event, such as the basement of the hotel where it occurred. This avoidance has become so pronounced that he now feels comfortable in only a very limited number of places, severely constricting his daily activities and interactions. The cycle of his symptoms has become self-reinforcing over time. His maladaptive strategies, like thought monitoring and sensory distraction, have not provided the relief he hoped for but instead have contributed to his negative appraisals about his body's unreliability and the sense that it is an enemy. These beliefs further heighten his feelings of threat and vulnerability, creating a vicious loop. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his quality of life had drastically diminished. His relationships with family members have suffered due to his withdrawn behavior, and he feels increasingly isolated and hopeless about ever regaining a sense of normalcy. Despite these challenges, John is determined to find ways to manage his symptoms and regain control over his life. He hopes for relief from the constant distress and the ability to trust his body again, allowing him to live without the overwhelming fear that has dominated his existence since the traumatic event. John's journey toward recovery will involve addressing his maladaptive coping mechanisms and challenging the negative beliefs that have taken root within him. By working through these issues, he aims to break the cycle of threat, memory intrusions, and negative appraisals that have been holding him back.
